name: Exponents
what_is_it: An exponent (or power/index) shows how many times a base number is multiplied by itself. In aⁿ, 'a' is the base and 'n' is the exponent. Grade 8 covers the exponent laws, squares and cubes, and an introduction to zero/negative exponents.
why_it_matters: Exponents let us write very large or very small repeated products compactly, and they underpin scientific notation, compound growth, area/volume formulae, and algebra in later grades.
key_vocabulary: Base — the number being multiplied repeatedly
Exponent/Power/Index — how many times the base is multiplied by itself
Square number — a number multiplied by itself once, e.g. 5² = 25
Cube number — a number multiplied by itself twice, e.g. 4³ = 64
core_concept: aⁿ = a × a × a ... (n times). Exponent laws let us simplify expressions without expanding every multiplication.
rules: Same base multiplication: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ
Same base division: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ
step_by_step_method: STEP 1: Check whether the bases are the same — laws only apply directly to matching bases.
STEP 2: Identify the operation (multiply, divide, or a power of a power).
STEP 3: Apply the matching exponent law to combine the exponents.
STEP 4: Simplify the final exponent; evaluate the number if required.
fast_method: When you see the SAME base being multiplied or divided, ignore the base and just add or subtract the exponents. Don't expand the whole multiplication.
why_fast_method_works: Multiplying powers of the same base is just stacking more copies of the base together — the total count of factors is the sum of the individual counts, which is exactly the exponent rule.
common_mistakes: Adding exponents when bases are different (e.g. 2³ × 3² ≠ 6⁵).
Multiplying the base by the exponent instead of applying the power (2³ ≠ 2×3).
Forgetting a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero base, not 0.
Mixing up (aᵐ)ⁿ (multiply exponents) with aᵐ × aⁿ (add exponents).
memory_trick: "Multiply → ADD. Divide → SUBTRACT. Power of a power → MULTIPLY." (Same operation family stays consistent: × goes with +, ÷ goes with −.)
visual_explanation: A repeated-multiplication chain diagram: 3⁴ shown as 3×3×3×3, next to 3² as 3×3, combined into one chain of six 3's to visually prove 3⁶.
mastery_check: Mastered when a student applies the correct exponent law automatically based on the operation shown, and can explain in words why the law works rather than just memorising it.
